text: Text and CSV files look almost identical from the outside, but Power BI treats them very differently depending on what's actually inside. Let's connect to one and see exactly how it decides.
Get data, Text CSV, browse to the file. Same pattern as every connector we've covered.

Here's our Financial Sample data again, this time saved as a CSV. Because Power BI found a comma separating every value, it shows you three settings: File Origin, Delimiter, and Data Type Detection — plus a full preview of the actual columns.

Delimiter is usually detected correctly, but you can override it. Comma, tab, semicolon, a custom character you type in yourself — even fixed-width columns, for files with no separator character at all.

Data Type Detection controls how hard Power BI works to guess each column's type. The default samples the first 200 rows — fast, but it can guess wrong if your data changes further down. Based on entire data set is slower, but safer.

Now here's the same connector, pointed at a plain text file with no delimiter at all — just two lines of prose. No Delimiter option, no Data Type Detection. Every line just becomes its own row, in a single column. That's the whole distinction: CSV is really just text with a delimiter Power BI could detect.

One connector, two experiences, and it all comes down to whether Power BI finds a delimiter inside the file. Next lesson, we connect to something with a lot more structure built in from the start: SQL databases. See you there.
